reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The alert matches the verified input on the type of action, an evacuation warning. Severity Severe, Urgency Expected and Certainty Likely are within what the input supports. However, the alert never names the hazard (the Kenneth Fire) and never says which places the warning covers. It says only 'in your area', while the verified input limits the warning to people near Calabasas, Agoura Hills and West Hills. The drafter should add both.

objections.issue: The alert does not name the hazard. The verified input says the warning is for the Kenneth Fire, but the headline and description name no fire or hazard. Recipients cannot tell what threat the warning is about.

reviews.summary: Delivery checks pass: English is GSM-7, 516 characters, 6 pages, under the 15-page cell broadcast maximum, and the GENERIC profile requires no languages. The first page fails the readability check. At 93 GSM-7 characters per page, page 1 holds only the preamble about the bulletin and the 10 km area. objections.issue: The first cell broadcast page (93 GSM-7 characters) does not carry the hazard or the action. Page 1 reads roughly 'This is a Province of Ontario emergency bulletin which applies to people within ten (10) kil'. The incident and the key instruction ('DO NOT need to take any protective actions', 'NO abnormal release') do not appear until pages 2-5. A reader who sees only page 1 learns there is an emergency near a nuclear station but not what happened or what to do. That invites alarm and calls.
objections.fix: Put the hazard and action in the first 93 characters. For example: 'Pickering Nuclear Station incident: NO radioactive release. NO action needed by public now.' Then follow with the area (within 10 km) and the media instruction. Keep the total at 15 pages or fewer.

reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: The Korean text is UCS-2, 78 characters over 2 pages, well under the 15-page limit, and the GENERIC profile requires no languages, so delivery is fine. The problem is content: the message never names the hazard. It says only that a 경계경보 (alert-level warning) was issued for Seoul and tells people to prepare to evacuate. It does not say what the threat is, where to go, or how. Readers of the first page cannot tell why they should act. The drafter can fix this by stating the hazard and a concrete action early in the text.

objections.issue: The hazard is never named. The text gives only the warning level (경계경보 발령) and a vague action (prepare to evacuate) with no destination or method. A handset reader, and especially the first page, therefore carries neither the hazard nor an actionable instruction. That risks public confusion rather than protective action.
objections.fix: Put the hazard type (for example, the specific threat behind the 경계경보) and a concrete action (for example, where to shelter or evacuate to) in the opening words, so both fall within the first UCS-2 page of about 41 characters. A suggested shape is: '[위험 유형] 경계경보: 서울지역 주민은 즉시 가까운 [대피소/지하시설]로 대피하십시오'. Move the time and the priority for children and the elderly after that.

round1.name: Arabic language reviewer
round1.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning across the headline, description and instruction. The hazard is the same: rain from convective clouds (السحب الركامية), light to moderate and heavy at times. The day (Saturday), the times (13:30 to 21:00) and the areas (some eastern, southern and western areas and parts of the interior) all match. The protective action also matches: take care outdoors or while driving during rain, and follow official updates at the same URL. I found no difference in meaning. The Arabic was produced by machine translation, so a named person who reads Arabic must still review and approve it before release. I cannot approve it.

round2.summary: Nothing within the issuing-authority mandate is wrong. The sender is in the issuer register at level 1, and its entry covers all areas and all categories. round2.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
round2.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present. Both use the right encoding (Arabic UCS-2, English GSM-7). Both are well under the 15-page maximum (en 3 pages, ar 6 pages). However, neither language gives recipients an action to take. The text describes the hazard (convective clouds, rain possibly heavy) and the time it is in effect, then ends. The first page therefore carries the hazard but not the action. The drafter can fix this.

objections.issue: Neither the English nor the Arabic phone text contains any recommended protective action. The message gives the hazard, areas and validity time, then stops, so the first page carries no action. Cell broadcast text may be truncated or read only on its first page, so essential information, including what to do, should come first.
objections.fix: Add a short protective instruction in both languages and place it early, within the first page. For example in English: 'Avoid valleys and flooded roads, drive carefully.' Add the Arabic equivalent. In Arabic, put it near the start of the message, since UCS-2 pages hold only about 41 characters. Shorten the area list if needed so that hazard and action both fit on page 1.
